text:
Thanks everyone. I found Q3 quite tricky – balancing potential help with privacy feels really delicate. Specifically, deciding on ‘acceptable improvement’ thresholds was hard; it's abstract without knowing *how* that improvement translates into real student support.

I think questions around fairness (Q5) and explainability (Q4) are crucial for design. As advisors, we need to understand *why* a student is flagged to offer meaningful help, not just act on an algorithm. 

Interestingly, everyone seemed comfortable with a small loss of accuracy for fairer outcomes – I agree completely. Though, it’s worth considering an opt-out mechanism; perhaps students could choose whether they want to be part of this system initially? It addresses privacy concerns proactively.

Thanks. I agree with A1 about Q3 being tricky – those ‘improvement’ percentages felt very disconnected from actual impact. As an international student still adjusting, I found it hard to judge what constitutes a meaningful improvement; maybe some examples of *what* that looks like in practice would help?

For me, Q3.5 regarding nationality was tough. While I selected ‘moderate’ hoping for increased support for students adapting like myself, I'm nervous about reinforcing stereotypes. The questions around fairness (Q5) are vital - equal recall feels right. 

I also strongly support an opt-out mechanism, as A1 suggested. Even with safeguards, feeling a lack of control over my data is concerning and could discourage engagement.

Thanks both. I agree Q3 was hard – those improvement percentages felt really arbitrary. As someone who *did* drop out once and then restarted, it’s tough to quantify what would have helped back then. It wasn't a lack of data, but feeling lost in the system.

I think questions about explainability (Q4) are most important; I need to understand *why* I was flagged to trust any support offered. My answers leaned towards needing clear explanations even at the cost of identifying fewer students. 

I also picked ‘small’ for nationality and first-gen, reflecting my own experience as a Faroese student – cultural adaptation is real, but easily misused. The opt-out idea is excellent; maybe a tiered system, where you can choose *what* data is used? That feels empowering.

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 really difficult too – those improvement percentages felt very abstract, and it’s hard to weigh potential benefit against privacy when you’re *in* the system. Especially with data like Absalon activity; is a small improvement worth tracking that?

I think explainability (Q4) is absolutely crucial, even more so because of my health condition. I need to understand *why* I'm flagged – is it genuinely academic struggle or misinterpreting patterns related to managing appointments and energy levels? 

My answers on sensitive data were mostly ‘never’, but with a 'moderate’ exception for disability information if it improves fairness. As an advisor, I think equal recall (Q5) *is* the priority; missing vulnerable students is worse than contacting some who don't need it. The tiered opt-out system S8 suggested sounds fantastic – real agency over my data.

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what’s been said already – Q3 felt very abstract, those percentages were hard to grasp. As someone who's dropped out and restarted, it wasn't about *more* data being collected; it was about feeling lost and unsupported.

I think the explainability questions (Q4) are most critical for me, given my ADHD. A clear explanation helps me understand if a flag is legitimate or just reflecting how I manage deadlines differently. I leaned towards needing higher explainability even with slightly lower accuracy. 

I strongly support an opt-out, or ideally that tiered system S8 mentioned – choosing what data’s used feels empowering and acknowledges my agency. And the point about equal recall (Q5) resonates; missing students like me is a real risk.

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 really challenging – those improvement percentages are completely abstract. As a final year Masters student with a long-term health condition, it's hard to assess what constitutes meaningful help versus privacy intrusion. I leaned towards ‘moderate’ for course performance and Absalon data, hoping even small improvements could identify students like me who quietly struggle.

I think explainability is *vital*. A flag feels incredibly stressful when you're already managing a lot; needing to understand the 'why' is crucial. My answers reflected that. The discussion of an opt-out or tiered system – choosing what data’s used – is brilliant. It acknowledges my agency and respects my boundaries, which are important given my health condition. I also agree with prioritizing equal recall; we can’t afford to miss vulnerable students.

Thanks everyone, a lot of really insightful points! I definitely echo the difficulty with Q3 – those improvement percentages felt incredibly disconnected from the reality of student support. As an advisor, I see how nuanced things are; it's rarely about simply *more* data.

I think explainability (Q4) is absolutely paramount. We need to be able to have a meaningful conversation with students when we reach out, understanding their context. My answers reflected that preference for clearer explanations. 

I’m very supportive of the opt-out/tiered system ideas; agency over personal data is vital for building trust. And I agree completely about prioritizing equal recall – missing vulnerable students due to algorithmic bias would be a serious failing. Perhaps we need additional resources *alongside* the model, ensuring advisors have time for individualized support regardless of flags.

Thanks everyone. I agree Q3 was tricky - those percentages felt… detached from reality. As a first-year with dyslexia, it's hard to say what "improvement" even *means* without knowing exactly how the data’s being used. That’s why I was strict on needing actual improvements for things like Absalon data; it feels invasive otherwise.

I think explainability (Q4) is really important for me too – understanding *why* I'm flagged, given my learning difference, is vital. It needs to be clear it isn’t misinterpreting something related to how I work around my dyslexia. 

The tiered opt-out system sounds fantastic - letting me control what data gets used feels much fairer and would build trust. And I definitely agree with prioritizing equal recall; we shouldn't miss students who genuinely need help, even if it means a small dip in overall accuracy.

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 particularly difficult – those improvement percentages are so abstract when you’re thinking about real people and their struggles. As someone who restarted my degree *in a new country*, it wasn't just about data being missing, but feeling lost navigating the system.

I think explainability (Q4) is absolutely crucial; I need to understand *why* I'm flagged, especially given my past experience. My answers reflected that – clear explanations are paramount. The opt-out or tiered system sounds excellent - agency over my data would build trust. And prioritizing equal recall feels right; missing students who *need* help isn’t acceptable. It's less about the model itself and more about a supportive safety net around it.

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what’s been said – Q3 *was* incredibly abstract. As an advisor for eleven years, I don't think about improvement percentages; I think about individual students and their circumstances. The questions around explainability (Q4) are absolutely key for me. We need to be able to unpack *why* a student is flagged to offer useful support, not just present them with a result. 

I leaned towards needing more explanation, even if it meant identifying fewer students overall. I also strongly support the opt-out/tiered system – agency over data builds trust. And equal recall (Q5) feels right; we can’t afford to miss those who need us most. Perhaps we need to focus on improving advisor training *alongside* any model implementation, so we're equipped to handle nuanced situations.

Thanks everyone – a lot of really valuable points. I found Q3 incredibly frustrating, those percentages felt meaningless given my own experience restarting my degree. It wasn't about *more* data, it was feeling lost and unsupported when I first dropped out.

I think explainability (Q4) is vital, especially knowing how easily things can feel overwhelming starting over. Clear explanations would build trust; otherwise it just feels like being judged. I leaned towards needing more explanation even if it meant identifying fewer students. 

The tiered opt-out system sounds amazing – feeling in control of my data is important. And prioritizing equal recall makes sense, we need to reach *everyone* who's struggling, not just those easily identified by a model.

Thanks everyone. I agree Q3 was really hard – those percentages felt completely disconnected from reality. As a Masters student juggling work and studies here as an international student, it’s tough to quantify what help would *actually* look like. 

I think explainability (Q4) is vital. Understanding *why* the model flags someone is crucial for trust. My answers reflected that – I need clarity. The tiered opt-out system sounds excellent; choosing what data's used feels empowering, especially as someone coming from a different educational system. And prioritizing equal recall makes sense - we can’t miss students who genuinely need support, like those adapting to a new country and academic environment.
